Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette:
Priya Chandrasekaran is a 32-year-old South Asian woman who serves as a city council member in a mid-sized American city. She came to the intake appointment dressed professionally but sat with her chair angled slightly toward the door, her eyes moving across the room before she settled into conversation. She described herself as someone who had always been driven and community-oriented, qualities that had carried her into public office in her late twenties. What she had not anticipated was that the same public life she had built would become the landscape in which her sense of safety completely collapsed.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Priya was attending a city-sponsored outdoor community festival in a downtown plaza - an event she had helped organize and was scheduled to speak at. Without warning, a gas main beneath the plaza ruptured and ignited. The explosion and subsequent fire moved through the crowd rapidly. Priya was close enough to feel the pressure wave knock her sideways and to watch, in the seconds that followed, people running in every direction through smoke and flame. She described being temporarily disoriented, unable to locate an exit, surrounded by screaming and the smell of burning. She eventually made it out through a side street, physically unharmed but having witnessed severe injuries to others around her. Several attendees were hospitalized. One did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Priya noticed that the world she returned to felt fundamentally altered. She had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought and more like a bodily certainty, that the world is a dangerous place and that safety is always provisional. She was certain that she had to be on guard at all times, because what happened in that plaza - an ordinary afternoon, a civic celebration - had demonstrated to her that catastrophe requires no warning and no logic. The conviction that you never know what can happen next was not, for Priya, a philosophical abstraction; it was something she had lived through in a public square on a Tuesday afternoon.

She began mapping every room she entered for exits. At council chambers, she knew which door opened fastest and which hallway led to the street. At restaurants, she would not sit until she had identified a clear path out. Unfamiliar venues presented a particular problem - she had stopped attending events at locations she had not previously visited, because she could not assess the danger in advance. This had consequences that extended well beyond her personal comfort. Council members are expected to appear at ribbon cuttings, town halls, and community gatherings across the district, and Priya had declined or delegated an increasing number of these engagements. Colleagues had begun to notice. She had attributed her absences to scheduling conflicts, but she understood that the explanation was wearing thin and that her effectiveness in office was being quietly compromised.

She also reported becoming hypervigilant toward the people around her, particularly in crowds, scanning faces and body language for signs of threat. She described this not as paranoia but as due diligence - a reasonable response to having learned what crowds can become. At night, this vigilance intensified; she found it genuinely harder to feel safe after dark, and her sleep had become fragmented. She had stopped exercising in the way she once had, avoiding any situation that placed her body under physical stress, because the elevated heart rate and shortness of breath felt too close to what she had experienced during the explosion.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a vote she had missed entirely - the first in her tenure - because it was scheduled at a venue she had never visited and could not bring herself to enter. She sat in her car outside the building for twenty minutes and then drove home. She described the shame of that evening with more visible emotion than anything else she disclosed. She was not sure, she said, whether she was hoping to feel safe again or whether she had simply accepted that she never fully would. What she did know was that she could not continue to serve her constituents from a distance, and that something had to change.
